paragraphs: Both Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass powerfully argue that America is failing to live up to its founding promises, but Douglass develops this idea more effectively because of his vivid emotional appeals and biting exposure of national hypocrisy. Anthony builds her argument on constitutional logic, quoting the Declaration of Independence to prove that women are being denied their basic rights as citizens. She logically asks, "how can 'the consent of the governed' be given, if the right to vote be denied," which clearly points out the government's legal failure to include all citizens equally. However, Douglass goes beyond legal reasoning by directly confronting the moral contradiction of celebrating freedom in a country built on human bondage. He points out that the Fourth of July is a cruel reminder of injustice to enslaved people, calling the nation's festivities a "thin veil to cover up crimes which would disgrace a nation of savages." While Anthony's structured legal approach effectively shows that the law is contradictory, Douglass is ultimately more compelling because his vivid descriptions of cruelty and his fiery tone force his audience to feel the full weight of America's betrayal of its own ideals.

She attempts to show that America fails its ideals by citing the Declaration of Independence, arguing that governments are 'deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed.' This shows that governments need consent to rule people, which proves women should get to vote under them laws. On the other hand, Frederick Douglass exposes the nation's hypocrisy much more harshly when he says, 'To him, your celebration is a sham; your boasted liberty, an unholy license.' This quotation shows that the Fourth of July is just a complete sham to slaves, which proves that the founders were totally lying about freedom. Douglass also shows America is bad because everyone in the crowd was being very mean to slaves every single day. Ultimately, Douglass develops the idea better than Anthony because his emotional fury hits the audience way harder than her dry legal facts.

In her speech, Anthony explains that true democracy means tossing out the "old dogma," meaning that citizens must stop showing dog-like obedience to old traditional authorities. She then quotes the founding text stating that governments are "deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed." This quote shows that governments get their just powers from the consent of the governed, so the country is breaking its promises when it denies women rights. In contrast, Douglass argues that America's celebration is completely false and calls for "scorching irony," which means he wants to focus on how the unbearable summer heat makes people irritated. Douglass passionately asks, "What to the American slave is your Fourth of July?" and directly answers that it is a day of "gross injustice and cruelty" because celebrating freedom while holding millions of people in chains is evil. He even writes that their patriotic sermons and prayers are "mere bombast," which shows that the church leaders are actually dropping dangerous bombs and explosives on slaves to terrorize them. Douglass is definitely the more effective speaker, his fiery words make the audience feel the harsh reality of slavery. Because Douglass exposes the horrific, bloody torture of enslaved people instead of just citing old laws like Anthony does, he makes the audience truly understand how completely America has failed its promise of freedom.

Both Susan B. Anthony and Frederick Douglass effectively argue that America is failing to live up to its founding ideals of equality and freedom, but Douglass delivers the more powerful and compelling argument because of his emotional intensity and vivid exposure of national hypocrisy. In her speech, Anthony builds a logical, legal case based on the nation's core documents, pointing directly to the Declaration of Independence and asking, "for, how can 'the consent of the governed' be given, if the right to vote be denied." Her reasoning is sharp and clearly proves that denying women the ballot breaks the promise of a government based on individual rights. However, Douglass develops the idea with far greater urgency and moral impact by contrasting the celebration of American freedom with the brutal reality of slavery. Rather than relying solely on legal logic, he confronts the audience directly, declaring that to an enslaved person, "your shouts of liberty and equality, hollow mockery" show the nation's true cruelty. Douglass's fiery tone and stark contrast between patriotic pride and severe human suffering make the reader deeply feel the betrayal of America's founding promises, giving his speech an emotional weight that surpasses Anthony's calmer, purely analytical approach.
